title: HTML Links
summary: A link takes the reader to another page or another part of the same page.
introduction: A link takes the reader to another page or another part of the same page. Think of a link as a signpost. Its words say where it goes, and its href value gives the address. Make a few clear signposts.
learningObjectives: Create links with absolute and relative URLs
Link to a section of a page and open links in a new tab safely
Write link text that is descriptive out of context

blocks.text: Everything between `` and `` becomes clickable; `href` (hypertext reference) is the destination.

An **absolute** URL includes the protocol and domain (`https://example.com/about.html`). A **relative** URL is resolved against the address of the current page, which keeps links working when you move the whole site to another domain.

rows: Same folder as the current page
`./` means the current folder (same as above)
Leading slash: from the site root, regardless of current folder

blocks.text: Links that work on your computer but break online are almost always caused by paths. `C:\Users\me\site\about.html` only exists on your machine; use relative paths and the same folder structure on the server.
Linking to a section of a page
Give the target element an `id` and link to it with `#id`. This works within the current page and across pages (`page.html#section`).

blocks.text: Opening links in a new tab

`target="_blank"` opens the destination in a new tab. Add `rel="noopener"` so the new page cannot access your page through `window.opener`; modern browsers do this by default, but writing it explicitly is still good practice. Use new tabs sparingly: users expect links to open in the same tab, and the Back button stops working across tabs.

blocks.text: `mailto:` opens the user's email program, `tel:` dials on phones, and the boolean `download` attribute asks the browser to save the file instead of displaying it.
When an image is the only content of a link, its `alt` text becomes the link text, so describe the destination ("Home page"), not the picture.
Screen-reader users often jump from link to link, hearing only the link text. "Click here" and "read more" tell them nothing. Describe the destination instead.

rows: `Click here to see the pricing`

blocks.title: Links versus buttons
blocks.text: A link takes the user somewhere; a button performs an action (submit, open a menu, play). Using `<a href="#">` as a button breaks keyboard behaviour and confuses assistive technology. If it does something rather than going somewhere, use `<button>`.
